name: Beth Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, governments or political parties. We don’t sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, and I've only been a junior manager for eight months, supervising five reception administrators inside a large equipment-hire company after the old records office was centralised. I've got a bachelor's degree, but I still need my boss to check the leave cover because I mix up which sites need two people, and I don't use AI at all. My partner has stopped warehouse work because of his knees, our two children are grown and living elsewhere, and my 2,850 take-home pays almost all our 2,800 monthly costs, including rent and annual bills. We've got 1,200 saved, few similar jobs nearby, and I keep saying I'd like to finish at 65 without having worked out whether we could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad we can concentrate on getting the cover right instead of changing the screen again. I'd keep that fairly quiet, because I don't want the younger staff thinking I resent them understanding things faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about my January confirmation review because I'm not yet quick or reliable at every part of this job. We have only 50 left in a normal month, and 1,200 doesn't cover even half a month of our full costs. AI doing little doesn't make my mistakes cost less. I couldn't comfortably lose the pay even for a short time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my boss this week to identify the two leave-cover mistakes I most need to stop making. I'd keep a paper checklist beside the existing scheduling screen and ask her to check Friday's plan during our already scheduled paid review, without adding unpaid work or assuming extra training hours. At home we'd keep putting the usual 50 monthly into savings while my wage lasted, and I'd keep the current job through the first year if the company confirmed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though not because I think a machine is about to take over tomorrow. I sometimes rehearse the cover question on the bus as if I'm about to sit an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner after a bad day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it was busy, then admit I'd needed the plan checked again. He's proud I got the job, which makes it harder to say I haven't properly got the hang of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the younger staff for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do ask where something is on the screen, and they're decent about it. I wouldn't ask them to sign off a staffing decision that's my responsibility, or call a helpful answer a promotion they haven't been paid for.

say: I'd welcome concentrating on **leave cover** instead of another screen change.
I'd avoid making **younger staff** feel blamed for understanding things faster than I do.
think: I worry about my **confirmation review** because I'm still unreliable at parts of the job.
Our **50 monthly surplus** and 1,200 savings leave no comfortable room for even a short loss of pay.
do: Ask my **boss** for the two priority cover errors and use a paper checklist beside the existing screen.
Use the existing **paid Friday review** for checking, without assuming extra training time or unpaid work.
Continue the usual **50 monthly saving** while paid and keep the job through the first year if confirmed.
feel: **Anxious**, rehearsing work questions on the bus.
S0.quote: AI doing little doesn't make my mistakes cost less.
fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** comes from junior performance risk and a near-zero household surplus rather than imagined radical change.
She seeks **supervision** inside an existing paid review and distinguishes colleagues' informal help from decision responsibility.

steps.text: Use a paper leave-cover checklist and the existing paid Friday review
Continue the usual 50 monthly savings transfer while paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should tell reception staff and managers what the new system means for hours and jobs. I'd want the union involved before anybody signs something they don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect my small supervisory post to be an early saving, because most of it is checking cover, writing updates and answering queries. Being a beginner at 58 doesn't leave me with a hidden specialist skill to offer instead. I think the pay could go, and that thought would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call the union office this week and ask whether my grade is covered, what joining costs and whether it could represent a new member in a future staffing change. I'd join only after those answers, with dues capped at 20 monthly from cancelling our 30 television package, leaving 10 more cash each month. In the first year I'd bring any proposed contract change to an adviser before signing, and ask my boss for explanations on paper rather than pretend I understood an AI system. I wouldn't count a promised conversation as a guarantee the union could save my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, with that tight feeling when the post lands on the mat. I'm slow at learning the job, and now I imagine the job disappearing before I finish learning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI to keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on my own; I'd be afraid of sending a reply I hadn't really written or checked. I'd ask what the company required, but I can see myself delaying that conversation, which doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might explain the union answers with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter could sit beside me while I read them, if she had an evening free. That would be help reading, not a promise that she could replace my wage or pay the rent.

say: I'd ask for clear answers about **hours and jobs** for both reception staff and managers.
I'd want **union involvement** before people sign changes they don't understand.
think: I expect my **supervisory post** to be an early saving because checking, writing and answering queries dominate it.
I have no **hidden specialist skill** to fall back on, and possible pay loss would keep me awake.
do: Ask the **union** about grade coverage, dues and future representation before joining.
Join only with satisfactory answers and **dues up to 20**, funded by cancelling the 30 monthly television package.
Bring proposed **contract changes** for advice before signing and request paper explanations of company requirements.
feel: **Alarmed and tense**, fearing the job will disappear before she has learned it.
S1.quote: I'm slow at learning the job, and now I imagine the job disappearing before I finish learning it.
fieldNote: Her **union enquiry** separates eligibility and representation from joining; the fee cap has a specific spending source.
She admits **avoidance** of AI requirements and does not give herself an implausibly quick technical reinvention.

steps.text: Ask about union coverage and join only under the stated representation and 20 dues gates
Cancel the 30 monthly television package to fund capped union dues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people shouldn't be left to disappear between losing work and being old enough for whatever support exists. I'd want the company to explain leaving payments to us face to face, not put a link in an email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty in 2028 and I'd expect the checking and messages that make up my job to go then, not when robots arrive in 2031. My partner has no wages, and I don't know of a pension I could claim at sixty. Our 1,200 wouldn't cover two weeks of full costs if my pay ended. I can't see a funded way through the years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my daughter now to spend one evening helping me list our rent, bills and accounts, but I'd ask rather than assume she could do it. In the first year after AGI, if I lost the wage, I'd go to the community advice centre with that list and ask someone to help with eligible support applications and any rent-relief request. I'd ask the company for my actual leaving-payment calculation and the union what representation was available, without counting money until entitlement and payment dates were confirmed. I honestly don't know what we'd do if those answers came back with no income; I wouldn't resign or tell the landlord I had money coming when I didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, because I can name people to ask but not a payment that would keep us housed. I picture opening the rent letter and then putting it under another letter, which is exactly the wrong thing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children take you in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to ask, and both live in small rented places with their own bills. My grown children live in small rented homes, so I can't put a spare bedroom into our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you and your partner take physical work until robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His knees stopped his warehouse job, and I'm not going to budget a lifting wage for him. I could ask about vacancies I'd actually be fit to do, but I have no offer, no agreed hours and no wage to put against the rent.

say: I'd oppose people losing support between **job loss** and later-life eligibility rules.
I'd ask for **face-to-face explanations** of leaving payments rather than an unexplained email link.
think: At **sixty**, I expect my thinking work to go before robots, with no known pension I can claim then.
Our **1,200 savings** cannot cover two weeks of full costs, and I see no funded route through the following years.
do: Ask my **daughter** for one evening listing household bills and accounts, without assuming her time or money.
Take the list to **community advisers** after wage loss for eligible support applications and a rent-relief request.
Request actual **leaving calculations** and union advice, counting no payment before entitlement and dates are confirmed; remain employed while possible.
feel: **Panicked**, able to name requests but unable to identify a funded housing plan.
S2.quote: My grown children live in small rented homes, so I can't put a spare bedroom into our plan.
fieldNote: Her **requests for help** are concrete, but she openly lacks a viable income bridge and does not count unconfirmed support.
She rejects an invented **physical-work fallback** for her partner's knees or herself without an offer, hours and a wage.

steps.text: Ask her daughter to help list rent, bills and household accounts
Request application help and rent relief through community advisers after wage loss
Ask the union what representation can cover the actual leaving-payment calculation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years ought to be enough time for the company and public authorities to explain the gap, even if it doesn't make the gap small. I'd support a union request for income protection for older staff who can't simply retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 in 2031, two years short of the age I've been saying I'd finish, but that age is a wish, not an entitlement I've checked. I still expect the desk work to go in 2031, before the 2034 robots. Five years gives me time to ask the questions without the rent already being late, but I don't yet have an answer that pays it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request written statements from every pension scheme I've paid into now, asking the earliest payable age, the amount after deductions and any penalty for drawing earlier. I'd take those statements and the budget to a free union advice appointment only after confirming they covered my grade and charged no fee. Over the preparation years I'd cancel the 30 television package and save that money with the existing 50, making 80 monthly only while my wage continued. In the first year after AGI, if the job ended at 63, I'd apply for any support I actually qualified for and would draw a pension only after written eligibility and net payments, together with other confirmed income, covered our then-current costs; I'd assume no leaving award or family cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but less lost than in the two-year picture because I can start with the pension envelopes. Five years is time to get an answer, not proof that I'll like the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the union appointment if it wasn't free?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what no-fee service they could refer me to instead. I wouldn't agree to a bill when we've only got 50 spare each month before any changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra saving achieve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 80 a month for sixty months it would add 4,800 if the wage and costs held, before emergencies. That's useful, but it wouldn't turn two years without a wage into a funded retirement.

say: I'd ask **employers and authorities** to explain the income gap facing older workers.
I'd support union demands for **income protection** where losing work doesn't mean being able to retire.
think: At **63**, I'd still expect my desk work to go; my hoped-for finishing age isn't a checked entitlement.
Five years permits **earlier questions**, but I don't yet have a confirmed income answer for the rent.
do: Request written **pension ages** and net amounts, including early-draw penalties, and obtain union advice only after confirming coverage and no fee.
Cancel the **30 television package** and save 80 monthly while wages last, including the existing 50.
Claim only eligible **support or pension** after job loss; draw pension only when confirmed eligibility and net household income cover actual costs.
feel: **Alarmed but less lost**, with time to open and understand the pension envelopes.
S3.quote: Five years is time to get an answer, not proof that I'll like the answer.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **age 63** from her unverified hope of finishing at 65 and never assumes a pension or leaving award.
The **80 saving** combines a real cut with the existing surplus; her 4,800 projection explicitly depends on wages, costs and emergencies.

steps.text: Request free union advice only after confirming grade coverage and no fee
Save 80 monthly while paid, combining the released 30 with the existing 50
Apply for support only under actual eligibility after wage loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the ten-year picture might let some people finish their working lives before the full change, but not everyone at my age has the money. I'd want pension information people can understand while they still have time to question it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 in 2036, and I'd hoped to stop at 65, so this is the first picture where the dates might work in my favour. I can't say I'm safe until I know whether income after stopping would pay our rent and bills. If it wouldn't, I'd still need work at 68 just when AGI threatened this job, and my partner's knees wouldn't improve because the date changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the same written pension eligibility, net amounts and deductions now, and ask a no-fee community adviser to compare them with our real costs before deciding any leaving date. I'd keep working while the job and my health allowed, continuing the ordinary 50 monthly saving rather than promise ten years of wages. I'd stop at 65 only if written pension terms and other confirmed household income covered costs with room for unexpected bills; otherwise I'd revise the date and seek eligible support rather than assume I could finish. In the first year after AGI I'd check the actual income and rent again, whether already retired or still looking for work, and apply for support only if eligible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious rather than panicked, because retirement before 2036 is possible, although not paid for just by wishing. I'd like to be able to look forward to a birthday without asking what bill it leaves behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would stopping at 65 mean you had brought retirement forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's the age I've been talking about already, and I'm not moving it earlier here. I might have to move it later if the numbers don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner after getting the figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lay the papers out and say what was confirmed, what was only an estimate and which bills we still couldn't cover. I'd ask him to look with me, rather than tell him I'd solved retirement because somebody printed an age on a statement.

say: I'd say some people can **finish before AGI**, while others of the same age still lack the money.
I'd ask for **plain pension information** early enough for people to question it.
think: At **68 in 2036**, the timing might favour my existing hope to stop at 65.
I still need **confirmed affordable income**; otherwise I'd require work as AGI threatens the job, with my partner unable to return.
do: Obtain written **pension terms** and no-fee community advice comparing net household income with actual costs before choosing a leaving date.
Keep working while **job and health** allow, continuing the existing 50 monthly saving without assuming ten more years of pay.
Stop at **65 only** with confirmed income covering costs and unexpected bills; otherwise revise the date and seek only eligible support.
feel: **Anxious rather than panicked**, seeing a possible but unconfirmed route to retirement before AGI.
S4.quote: I'd like to be able to look forward to a birthday without asking what bill it leaves behind.
fieldNote: Her **age arithmetic** is explicit: 58 now, 68 at AGI, with an existing hoped-for stopping age of 65 rather than earlier retirement.
The **retirement gate** requires written eligibility and sufficient net income, while community advice and support remain no-fee or eligibility-bound.

steps.text: Request no-fee community advice comparing written pension terms with household costs
Continue working and the ordinary 50 monthly saving while job and health allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be sixty with no proper cushion and no confidence I could find another management job nearby. A person to help me apply for support, written notice, and a union adviser who could check what the company owed me would help. I need a bridge made of actual payments, not another birthday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask why somebody's learning a junior job at my age before assuming I've been in charge for thirty years. Keeping the old records right didn't teach me how to manage five people, and I don't want to pretend it did. I want a fair chance to learn, not a medal for being old.

headlineQuote: I need a bridge made of actual payments, not another birthday.
portrait: Beth is **58**, a junior manager with a bachelor's degree who is still learning to supervise five reception administrators.
She and her **partner** rent their home, their children are grown, and his knee problems have stopped his warehouse work.
Her **low management pay** barely covers household costs, with 1,200 saved and few similar local vacancies.
She **never uses AI** and seeks practical union and family help, while treating retirement at 65 as an unfunded hope.
biggestWorry: I fear **AGI by 2028** most because I'd be sixty with thin savings and few local options.
whatWouldHelp: I need **application help**, written notice and a union check of the company's actual payment obligations.
